drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Customer support scenario. Policy says refunds above five hundred dollars need a human.
drills.answer_line: SAM: Right. A loses because PostToolUse fires after execution
drills.stem: Refunds above $500 need a human. A PostToolUse hook on process_refund posts an alert to finance whenever an over-$500 refund goes through. Over-limit refunds are still reaching customers. What should change?

options.A: Keep the hook and add an automatic reversal when the alert fires
options.B: Hook that intercepts process_refund before it runs, blocks over $500, tells agent to escalate_to_human
options.C: Add the limit to the system prompt in capitals with two few-shot examples
options.D: Intercept the call before it runs and block over-limit amounts with a generic "operation not permitted"

drills.why: B blocks before execution and redirects to escalation: both verbs. PostToolUse fires after the money moves; a generic error (D) leaves the agent no next step.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Customer support scenario. Choose two. Which two requirements should be enforced with Agent SDK hooks
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and C. A is outgoing-call interception
drills.stem: Choose two. Which two requirements should be enforced with Agent SDK hooks rather than system prompt instructions?

options.A: Refunds above $500 must never be issued without human approval
options.B: The agent should acknowledge frustration before proposing a fix
options.C: Third-party MCP order dates (Unix timestamps) must reach the agent in the same format as your own tools'
options.D: The agent should escalate when policy does not cover the customer's request

drills.why: A: checkable threshold with a financial consequence, intercepted before the call. C: PostToolUse normalisation of a server you cannot fix. B, D, E are judgement or style.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Code generation scenario. A developer spent an hour in Claude Code mapping a payments module
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. "Compare two approaches" plus "from the existing analysis"
drills.stem: After an hour mapping a payments module in Claude Code, the team wants to compare two testing strategies (contract tests vs property-based tests) and pick one. What should the developer do?

options.A: Start two new sessions, one per strategy, each mapping the module again so neither is biased
options.B: Use fork_session to create two branches from the existing analysis, one strategy in each
options.C: Try the first strategy in the current session, revert the files, then try the second
options.D: Ask the current session to describe both strategies and recommend one without writing tests

drills.why: Two approaches from a shared baseline is the fork case. A repeats an hour of work; C carries the first attempt's reasoning; D compares descriptions, not results.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Code generation scenario. Two weeks ago a developer ran a named Claude Code session
drills.answer_line: SAM: That's the miss I wanted to hear. Miss pattern four
drills.stem: Two weeks ago a named session analysed an auth service. Since then another team replaced the token library and rewrote most of the service's files. The developer wants to continue. What is the most reliable approach?

options.A: Resume the named session with --resume and list the changed files so it re-analyses them
options.B: Resume the named session and ask it to carry on
options.C: New session seeded with a structured summary of findings that still apply, reading the current code
options.D: Fork the old session so the original stays intact while the fork re-analyses

drills.why: Targeted re-analysis fits when prior context is mostly valid. Most files changed and the library was replaced, so nearly every tool result is stale.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Customer support scenario. A customer gives the name Jordan Lee
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. The customer knows who they are; one extra turn removes the guess.
drills.stem: A customer named Jordan Lee asks to cancel an order. get_customer returns three Jordan Lee accounts. The agent picks the one with an open order and sometimes cancels the wrong customer's order. What is the best fix?

options.A: Ask for another identifier (email or order number) on multiple matches, before any account action
options.B: Change get_customer to return only the highest-ranked match
options.C: Proceed with the most likely account and state its email in the reply so the customer can correct it
options.D: Have the agent rate its confidence in the match and ask only when it falls below 7

drills.why: One extra turn removes the guess. B hides ambiguity in the tool; D is self-reported confidence; C confirms only after acting: one wrong clause.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Customer support scenario. Choose two. Which two situations should trigger escalation
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and C. A is an explicit request: honour it now
drills.stem: Choose two. Which two situations should trigger escalation to a human?

options.A: Customer writes "I want to talk to a real person" about a duplicate charge the agent could refund in one step
options.B: Sentiment analysis scores the customer's last three messages as strongly negative
options.C: Request to transfer loyalty points to family; policy covers earning and redeeming, silent on transfers
options.D: The agent rates its own confidence in a refund decision as 5 out of 10
options.E: Customer annoyed a replacement is late, has not asked for a person, policy covers the case

drills.why: A is an explicit request: honour it now. C is a policy gap. Sentiment and self-rated confidence are unreliable; E is frustration within capability.

drills.question_line: SAM: A recall check before the tease. Pause and name the three topics, and the word in a stem
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Hooks, where the giveaway is timing.
drills.prompt: Name the three topics, and the word in a stem that gives each one away.
drills.answer: Hooks: timing. Sessions: how much changed. Escalation: whether the customer actually asked for a person.
